entry.title: Policy Language Models
entry.content:
This post introduces what I’m working on right now, Policy Language Models. The paper is linked at the end.

Updated August 2026, with the definitions stated in full, the experimental program, and its results.

The trajectory

Frontier large language models and the harnesses built around them can now tackle complex long-horizon problems, resolve software issues, conduct deep research, and drive hours-long sessions. These gains have largely come from inference-time scaling. Models are trained to spend more tokens deliberating, and ReAct systems extend that capability by interleaving reasoning with actions and observations. ReAct remains the dominant substrate for this work. We define a ReAct trajectory as a growing sequence of thoughts, actions, and observations.

In ReAct, the trajectory only grows, and LLM outputs degrade as the context window fills. The most popular general approach to solve this is context condensation or compaction, where context from user requests or agent trajectories is repeatedly summarized when it exceeds a length threshold. Unfortunately, context compaction loses information and therefore is not a good solution to this problem. Trajectories pushed to length fail in characteristic ways; the next section lists them, and the paper studies each. We believe these failures act as a dampener on reasoning LLMs, and that solving them will yield far more capable reasoners.

The failures are not only about length. A ReAct loop bundles two separable things, the capability of interleaving thought with code, and the protocol that ends the call: a disclosed round budget, an obligation to answer, a return channel, pressure at the end. Frameworks ship them fused, because a call that cannot end is useless to a caller who only receives a value. In my own runs the protocol failed on its own terms, sub-agents surrendering early and returning nothing, returning a progress report where an answer belonged, returning the literal string done. These are artifacts of the channel, not of the deduction, and they appear wherever the channel is present.

Where the trajectory fails

In both CoT and ReAct the model builds a single autoregressive line, and every step is produced by conditioning on the entire prefix. The clearest symptom is error propagation. A misread observation or a hallucinated step is never removed; even when the model questions it later, the append-only trajectory leaves the original in place, and the mistake keeps conditioning everything after it. The literature adds brittleness to small prompt changes, myopia and drift over long horizons, and a decision advantage that decays with length. We read these as one mismatch. The model keeps reaching for reasoning shapes the substrate cannot hold, it branches to weigh alternatives, reverts to undo a wrong step, and explores before committing, and every such move is flattened back into one forward sequence.

Exploration. The divergent move, floating an alternative or reasoning about hypotheses, is what a reasoner uses when direct deduction does not reach the answer. It buys coverage at the cost of stability: it opens regions of the problem without closing them, and past a balance point the unclosed excursions fragment the reasoning rather than enrich it. A molecular-structure account of long chain-of-thought treats the links between reasoning steps as bonds of differing strength and finds self-exploration to be the weakest of them; excessive exploration yields fragmented reasoning, and a deteriorated structure, once formed, is hard to restore. Methods that use exploration successfully converge only when an external controller supplies the convergence: self-consistency votes over independent samples, Tree-of-Thoughts adds a prune-and-backtrack controller, while unaided self-correction can regress rather than repair. Exploration is productive to the degree that it can be retracted.

Self-reflective strain. Retraction is the job of reflection, a later step reaching back to reexamine an earlier one, and models fail at it in a specific way. When the back-link reaches a load-bearing step it contradicts, the result is not repair. An early bias triggers excessive, circling reflection instead of a clean fix; once an error is in the chain the model resists correcting it and reinforces the flawed logic through further reflection; and the reconsideration that looks like self-correction rarely improves the answer. Resolving the strain is also not the same as repairing the reasoning: even when the model concludes an earlier step was wrong, it leaves the steps built on that premise largely unrevised, because it does not reliably know which later results descended from the faulty step. The intervention literature bears this out. Editing the error at its own origin reverses the final answer in under a quarter of cases, and the reliable escape is to discard the corrupted prefix and restart rather than patch it in place.

Capacity. All of this happens inside one context window shared by everything the trajectory does. Because the trajectory is one line, a reasoning shape is not additional structure but additional tokens, paid from the budget that must also hold the problem, the input, the observations, and the reasoning itself. The budget is smaller than advertised: performance is highest when relevant information sits at the ends of the input and degrades in the middle, most evaluated models fall below half their short-context baselines by 32K tokens once the task needs more than literal matching, and input length alone degrades performance by 14 to 85 percent even when the model retrieves everything perfectly. On the output side, models spend excessive reasoning tokens on problems that do not need them, and in ReAct every observation and tool result accumulates in the same window, none of it offloadable. A single trajectory is bounded on both sides, by how little of the window it can actually use and by how much of its own work it must keep there.

The sources for each of these findings are cited in the paper, linked at the end.

Taking work off the line

Recently, Zhang, Kraska, and Khattab introduced Recursive Language Models (RLMs), a general-purpose inference paradigm that dramatically scales the effective input and output lengths of LLMs. Their key insight is that an arbitrarily long prompt should not be fed directly into the neural network but should be treated as part of the environment the LLM interacts with, symbolically and recursively. An RLM exposes the same external interface as an LLM: a string prompt in and a string response out. Given a prompt \(P\), it initializes a REPL environment in which \(P\) is set as the value of a variable, and the model writes code that peeks into and decomposes \(P\), observes the effects of execution, and invokes the LLM itself on as many slices of the input as necessary. By treating the prompt itself as an external object and enabling symbolic recursion, RLMs tackle limitations of expressive power in recent work on coding agents, retrieval agents, and sub-agent delegation. What leaves the trajectory, however, is only the input/output processing. Thinking, exploration, reflection, action, and observation still accumulate on the root trajectory, and the thinking is still done the ReAct way.

The paragraph above is from my introduction, drafted early, and it reflects my understanding of RLMs at that time. The comparisons later in the post that speak of RLMs as data processing come from the same draft. I have kept them as written because the ideas in this post grew out of that reading; the next two paragraphs give the fuller one.

I first read this as a result about input processing, and the paragraph above still frames it that way. Zhang’s work over the summer makes the actual claim explicit, and it is about composition. A harness induces an equivalence relation over tasks: two problems that share latent structure, however different their vocabulary and their length, reduce to nearly the same token trajectory in the root, because the harness offloads the domain-specific material into sub-calls and exposes only the structure needed to choose the next operation. A good harness shapes each call so that every observation is, in his phrase, locally in-distribution. What he demonstrates is that training on short tasks generalizes to tasks eight to thirty-two times longer, and that training on one domain transfers to others. Input length is where this is measured. It is not what is being claimed.

This matters here because it is the strongest available statement of what a harness is for, and it is not the statement I was making. His invariant is a property of the model’s input distribution, that every call the model sees looks like something it was trained on. Ours is a property of the trajectory’s information state. Those are different objects, and most of this post is about the second one. He hedges the reach of his own conjecture, that the tasks people care about can “apparently almost always” be decomposed naturally, and he offers no characterization of the training set that would suffice; I read the hedges as honest rather than as an opening.

Policy Language Models

We introduce Policy Language Models (PLMs), a general-purpose meta-reasoning inference paradigm for scaling the reasoning power of LLMs. The key insights are that reasoning and expressing the computation for a task cost far fewer tokens than the LLM doing the task itself, and that the ability to express different computational shapes leaves room for neuro-symbolic programs authored by the PLM that do the task better than an LLM doing it autoregressively. Meta-reasoning is the reasoning behavior built on these two facts: reasoning intertwined with the computations it authors. This behavior sheds the failures plaguing ReAct while keeping all its benefits, offers additional benefits, and, we believe, carries a far higher ceiling for reasoning LLMs.

Call the main trajectory sufficient if no information added to it from the work done off it would significantly increase the information available to the LLM, and minimal if it is sufficient in the fewest tokens possible. We formally define meta-reasoning as the behavior that keeps the main trajectory sufficient and near-minimal by creating and delegating to computations and assimilating their work. A PLM has two parts: the harness, where computations are authored and run as policies in a persistent REPL environment, and the model, trained to achieve the meta-reasoning behavior.

What an RLM does for data processing, a PLM does for all the work that a trajectory would otherwise hold. Since data processing is a type of computation, RLM capabilities follow as a special case. The computations a PLM generates are called policies. These policies can be run, edited, and composed dynamically, which makes it easier to express and carry out the trajectory’s reasoning and work through them. The harness provides a small set of LLM primitives, which are the elementary capabilities of a reasoning LLM, enabling the PLM to create neuro-symbolic programs. An LLM policy is any policy that contains these primitives. Such a policy is programmed rather than called as a tool. By contrast, an RLM’s sub-call takes a query string under a system prompt fixed by its harness. This core distinction makes LLM policies more expressive than an RLM’s programs. Although delegation is easier for the trajectory because tool calls carry no reasoning overhead, building policies provides greater expressive power. Because the neural and symbolic parts are deeply integrated in our harness, this differs from RLMs, where it is akin to a tool call. As a result, a PLM can build a far greater variety of LLM policies than simple tool-call delegation allows.

Meta-reasoning requires the main trajectory to have control over all the work the harness performs. An RLM’s root trajectory lacks this control, by design and by intent. By design, a recursive sub-call is another RLM, so the root cannot vary what it may do beyond a certain extent, and the root does not have explicit control over its capabilities, including whether the sub-call delegates further. Deeper recursion has already been observed to degrade performance and increase cost. By intent, Zhang hypothesizes that frontier models are “severely underutilized due to sub-optimal use of individual language model calls” and proposes training models to decompose tasks such that each sub-task is in-distribution for a sub-call, with each sub-call autonomous over its piece. A PLM retains the aforementioned control because of how it must author policies: besides standard Python, it has access only to the LLM primitives defined above. So every neuro-symbolic policy is a program made of code and these elementary LLM capabilities.

Zhang proposed training models to decompose. We pose a different question: can an LLM be trained to author the neuro-symbolic program that solves the task? Decomposition is one type of neuro-symbolic program among many. The difference is that a decomposer must estimate what is in-distribution for its sub-calls, while the PLM must estimate the behavior of each of its LLM primitives and build programs around that behavior. A policy succeeds when it behaves as the PLM estimated it would, its code and its LLM primitives alike. In the same spirit, what Zhang asks of decompositions, we ask of neuro-symbolic programs at large.

A PLM reasons about the goal abstractly and expresses the computation as policies. It authors, runs, and edits them inside a REPL environment, composing sub-LLM calls into policies whose returns it constrains, and reasons onward from their results. Here, the PLM authors a single evolutionary policy that breeds candidate policies through sub-LLM builders, selects among them by played outcomes, and folds only gated winners into its deliverable.

What the substrate buys is also compounding. A policy authored once can be rerun, revised, and composed into larger ones, so the work of reasoning accumulates as artifacts rather than as tokens. The trajectory that once stretched to hold every reasoning structure within a context window can now express those structures as policies. The substrate alone, however, does not produce the behavior. In our experiments, current LLMs placed on the PLM harness do not spontaneously meta-reason, they grind the work inline out of habit, or scatter one-off delegations that are at best half-cooked. The disposition has to be trained in. We take that as the finding that matters: meta-reasoning is a trainable surface of improvement that today’s models have never been optimized for.

The harness

A PLM runs in a persistent programming environment \(\mathcal{E}\), a Python REPL whose state survives across rounds. Each round the model thinks, then acts through one code tool call that executes in \(\mathcal{E}\); the call’s printed output and errors are appended to the trajectory as the tool result, and RETURN(obj) ends the loop with its argument as the response. A PLM trajectory holds three things: the reasoning, the code, and the code’s output.

The @policy decorator turns a function or a class into a named artifact. It persists across rounds, holds global scope so it is used by name and never imported, can be edited in place and duplicated, and is identified by its source code, which is what persists, what is read back, and what is revised.

Three LLM policies are provided. llm is a single call. react_auto is an LLM with the python tool, run in ReAct rounds under the termination protocol, a disclosed round budget, a bound RETURN, pressure at the end, which is to say a conventional sub-agent. react is the same loop with the protocol removed: it runs exactly the rounds it is given and stops, still open, RETURN is not defined inside it, and it injects no text of its own, so every word in a stepped trajectory is either the author’s or the model’s. Every sub-llm call begins empty. Its prompts, its inputs, any helper or policy it will use, the decorator and the LLM policies themselves, are handed to it; nothing is ambient. A sub-call may run LLM policies of its own; nothing runs deeper.

A constraint is a typed class defining invariants on a computation’s output. It is compiled into the schema the call decodes under, so a violating structure cannot be emitted; the call yields the validated value, or None when the round budget ends without one, and policy code branches on the result.

Weaving makes the two products of a computation into ordinary objects. Messages pass by reference: a react run over a list leaves its turns on that list, and the list can be edited, pruned, restored, or handed to another policy as an object. State passes by ownership: a sub-agent’s namespace is a dictionary the caller holds, so everything the sub-computation defined, variables and functions alike, stays readable and callable after the call and between rounds, and granting is putting a key in that dictionary. There is no session object; a session is the pair of containers the author is holding.

The design has one organizing rule, and it is about information. Relative to the main trajectory, an artifact produced by work done off it is in one of four states: held, it is in the trajectory; handled, the trajectory knows it exists, roughly what it is, and how to reach it; latent, it is reachable but the trajectory never registered it; lost, unreachable, or recoverable only by paying its full price again. Sufficiency, from the definition above, is that everything that matters is held or handled, and the preference runs toward handled, since a handle costs a few tokens to carry and a few to cash in. Each capability exists to keep artifacts on the upper rungs. Weaving keeps a sub-computation’s trajectory handled rather than lost, the list is an object the policy holds. State weaving does the same for everything the sub-computation defined, the namespace being the caller’s dictionary. Constraints make a return’s shape known before it exists, so the handle describes its artifact. The react split keeps even an unfinished computation handled, since the policy can read the open trajectory and decide what happens next. Under the string contract the default is the opposite: the moment a call returns, everything but the returned string is lost. This is the sense in which the harness adds power, not raw ability on tasks, which the experiments below looked for and did not find, but control over what the work leaves behind.

The invariant, under pressure

Sufficiency is a state of the trajectory and the model together. Every artifact the run has produced is either in the trajectory’s tokens, or the model knows it: it knows what the artifact is and where it is, and it can use it without any further work. Knowing is a stronger condition than having access. The model can always open a sub-policy’s message list and read it, but until it has read it, it does not know what is in there, and the ladder calls that artifact latent. The knowledge also does not have to be written in tokens; some of it can be carried by the model’s weights and some by the trajectory. A trajectory is sufficient when everything that matters is in it or known, and minimal when it is sufficient in the fewest tokens.

The definition also says where sufficiency fails. A policy is neuro-symbolic code, and a computation stores more than what it was written to store: a verifier’s messages hold text no one reads, a variable holds a side effect, an intermediate value has a shape no one printed. The model does not know these by default, so a trajectory over such a computation is not sufficient until each of them is known or shown not to matter. Knowing also has levels. Information in the trajectory is the full level; below it sits the meta-information about that information, what an artifact is, where it is, and what using it costs, which is enough for the model to know the artifact without holding it. Assimilation is the behavior that produces this knowledge, and it is itself computation: computation about what a computation stored and what shape its products took. Each act of assimilation increases the information the trajectory carries about the artifacts the work produced, usually at the meta level, so an artifact becomes handled without being read in full, and that is how assimilation serves meta-reasoning. Reading a return, scanning a message list, checking what a variable holds are all assimilation at different grains. Proving the presence or absence of information is also assimilation: the proof is what lets the model move on, using the artifact or discarding it without reading it, because the question about it is settled. Delegation breaks sufficiency and assimilation restores it.

A long-context model has sufficiency without minimality, one window holding everything and losing whatever eviction takes. An aggressive offloader has minimality without sufficiency, a short root over sub-computations whose reasoning dies at the return. Zhang’s invariant, every observation locally in-distribution, says what the model must generalize over. It does not say what the root can still reach.

An RLM cannot express sufficiency, and the check is the contract, not a benchmark: rlm_query returns a string, and no channel returns the turns. A sub-call’s trajectory is invisible to the root, which holds only what the sub-model chose to say, where a PLM policy holds the trajectory itself, every turn the sub-model wrote, its code and its answers. Hidden reasoning tokens cross the wire for neither system, my own harness strips that field, so the comparison is over what actually crosses. Zhang notes that his roots keep printing task-specific information back into the main context, and calls it undesirable for generalization; I read it as a system straining against this missing channel.

Role authorship is the other half of the contract argument. Under the string contract the mapping from provenance to role is fixed by protocol, code output enters as tool or user material and an assistant turn can only be genuinely generated, while a PLM policy places any content under any role: a commitment the model appears to have made, an observation the environment appears to have produced, a system update arriving mid-history.

Why this pair is the objective: sufficiency is a per-step invariant with a whole-run consequence. The empty trajectory is sufficient. If every action either works inside the trajectory or delegates and then assimilates, then sufficiency holds at every round, and by induction the run never loses information it needed: from a sufficient state, whatever the system could do holding the whole computation tree, it can do from the state alone. This also makes it a usable training signal, since it can be checked at every round, while the task outcome arrives once at the end.

Two conjectures follow from minimality. When a sufficient trajectory is reduced to minimal, most of what remains is information about information, since a handle costs fewer tokens than the artifact it points to. The number of handles grows with the number of artifacts, not with their size, so the root’s length is governed by the structure of the computation tree rather than by its bulk; this is generalization in the amount of information. Handles also look similar across domains, since a handle records what an artifact is, where it is, and what it costs to use, whatever the artifact itself is; so the distribution the root is trained on shifts less across domains than the underlying content does; this is generalization in the domain of information. Where Zhang’s invariant makes every observation locally in-distribution, this one makes the root’s own content domain-invariant. The formal target is for the trajectory to be a sufficient state of the computation tree; the information-state literature defines states sufficient with respect to an environment, and the object here is different, a tree of computations that the trajectory itself authored.

What I set out to show, and what happened

The theory above has a companion claim, and it is the claim I spent the summer trying to establish. If a PLM can hold objects an RLM cannot, the space of policies it can author should be strictly larger in a way that shows up as capability. Write \(\Pi_X\) for the interaction structures a program can control under contract \(X\), and \(R(\pi)\) for the tasks a policy \(\pi\) gets right; a trained PLM covers the union of \(R(\pi)\) over the policies \(\theta\) can write. The prediction was that this union outruns what any decomposition-shaped system reaches. That would have been a direct challenge to Zhang’s conjecture.

I built three harnesses to test it. One is the full PLM harness. One is the same harness with exactly the beyond-string-contract surface removed, so a policy there is arbitrary code around string-in, string-out calls: the agentic region, and, with the round budget fixed, the system message withheld, and the namespace switch off, the RLM region. The third is a further restricted variant for a separate experiment. A test asserts the diff between them, so the boundary is materialized rather than promised.

The comparison did not go my way. On an interactive deduction task the best agentic policy scored 0.70 against the best PLM policy’s 0.60 over ten development instances, one instance apart, and pooled over every run the ordering holds at 0.80 against 0.53, with run-to-run variance large enough that the PLM arm scored five of six and then two of five on overlapping instances. One more number empties both figures of meaning as a barrier test: an offline pass over the ten knowledge books, done before any policy ran, put the task’s own ceiling at 0.616 under its action budget, because the books over-claim and the observations rule out the gold artifact in seven instances of ten. Both arms were pressed against noise in the data, not against either contract.

The emulation was harder to argue with. I flattened the PLM policy into its best string-contract form, everything it did but re-fed as one labeled transcript, and it reproduced the PLM maximum exactly on the iteration set, beat it on the full ten, and did it at sixty-four percent of that arm’s token cost. Instrumenting both arms said why. Graded against a reference table, re-feeding read the books at ninety-one percent exact-rule fidelity, precisely what the live agentic session read them at, while the best PLM arm sat at 77.2, and thirty-six of its thirty-eight lost rules came from a single instance where fidelity fell to 5.3 percent, a sixteen-round session in which the model simply stopped populating the namespace dict. A session pathology beat the PLM arm, not a reasoning deficit. Against my own case I will also record that those PLM arms never passed constraint and never made a protocol-bearing call, reading their answers out of the namespace after plain react rounds, so every loss on that side was authoring rather than a mechanism the contract had withheld.

Three constructed tasks stacked the mechanisms PLM has and the string contract does not, and none produced a gap I could defend. The first swung two thirds the wrong way on the small model and converged at ceiling on the larger one, where every arm finished perfect and the task stopped discriminating. The second scored zero everywhere, partly through difficulty and partly through a PLM-side degeneracy worth naming, one instance spending fourteen rounds refusing to call its own tool and asking me to run it and paste the result back. The third sat at chance in all four arms, and one of the four was RLM-shaped by construction, single-shot string calls over a context held as a REPL variable with no round budget exposed to the sub-call, so the comparison was never only against my own agentic region.

Two findings appeared that I was not looking for, and both cut against the theory. A fresh context per phase acts as an error reset, deleting the degeneracy a long session accumulates, so at small scale the boundaries I had counted as losses were doing repair; on the larger model the degeneracy is gone, the reset has nothing left to cure, and the sign moved without ever flipping my way. And curation is a liability when the distillation is noisy: the policy that pruned stale reports and told the model its state table was its memory scored zero, while the same composition with the raw reports left in the weave scored a third. The redundancy I removed was the redundancy the model repaired itself with.

One finding runs the other way, and it is about the protocol rather than the contract. On the qualifying model the naive bubble scored zero, piping its first observation straight into RETURN and quitting on all six instances, and the naive chopped arm scored 0.50, its bubbles satisfying the return obligation without performing the commit the task actually graded; ordinary code around the call repaired both to a clean sweep. The protocol tax is real, it is the only irreducible I saw bite at that scale, and it is the one most cheaply patched from outside. That is why the emulation ties.

The mechanism behind the null constrains everyone, not only me. Code computes whatever its inputs determine, which is why a solver inside a policy beats any amount of deliberation about the same clauses; but where a task’s difficulty is judgment rather than computation, the model is the only source, and a policy’s output distribution is a computable transformation of the conditionals it can elicit. A policy can select among samples, condition them differently, compose them, amplify them with a checker. It cannot create probability the model does not assign. At vanishing probability under every reachable conditioning, no shape helps; at decent probability, cheap shapes already win.

One thing escapes that argument, and it is a theorem. Give a policy a sound polynomial-time checker and \(k\) samples, and its success on an obligation is one minus the chance of \(k\) failures, so the region it handles reliably strictly contains the model’s own and tends to the model’s support as \(k\) grows. A harness moves a task to where the model is reliable; a verifying policy only needs it possible. Verification is also the top rung of a ladder, voting, search, invariant regulation, cross-examination, constrained decoding beneath it, each demanding a weaker symbolic object, and a policy is the closure of those generators under composition, not the list. Every rung has an output-side form that any coded harness owns, about which I claim nothing, and a trajectory-side form that only a participant in the computation owns. My probes exercised the output side almost exclusively, which is consistent with the nulls, and is exactly where the theory says a gap should not be.

What fell, exactly, is the prediction, that the larger authorable space shows up as an accuracy gap on tasks I could build and afford. The containment stands, an RLM decomposition is a PLM policy at the one level of nesting both systems actually run, call depth being fixed by my kernel as an experimental condition while orchestration depth stays unbounded on both sides. And the invariant stands. Sufficiency remains inexpressible under the string contract for the contract’s own reason, and assimilation, which sufficiency licenses, is the part of the idea the experiments never reached.

What is new here

The word first. Meta-reasoning is an old term, and this is not its classic sense. Russell and Wefald defined metareasoning as selecting which computations are worth running by their expected value, and De Sabbata et al. ported that sense to LLMs, training a model to spend its own reasoning tokens only where they pay. Both govern whether to compute. The definition above governs what the main trajectory must contain once the computation happens somewhere else. Where the distinction matters I say sufficiency rather than meta-reasoning, because the invariant, not the word, is the claim.

The neighborhood is crowded, and I want to be exact about it. Trained context economy exists: Context-Folding learns branch-and-fold operations by reinforcement, spawning a sub-trajectory for a subtask and collapsing it to a summary on return; CompactionRL trains self-summarization jointly with the task; MemAgent trains an overwrite memory that reads millions of tokens. ABBEL is the closest thing to the invariant in print: the agent’s history is replaced by a natural-language belief state trained with an accuracy grade and a length penalty, which is operationally a sufficient and near-minimal state as a training signal. Trained delegation exists too: Conductor trains a small model to author subtasks, prompts, and communication topologies for worker models. Nobody, myself included, can still claim training an agent to delegate and keep its context small as a contribution.

Four things in this post have no occupant that a systematic pass turned up.

The invariant itself. Sufficiency here is defined counterfactually against the off-trajectory work: the root is sufficient when no information from the work done off it would significantly add to what is available, minimal when sufficient in the fewest tokens, which makes the root a sufficient statistic of the whole computation tree, stated as one trainable criterion. ABBEL grades its belief against environment unknowns in interactive games, not against computations the root created, and Context-Folding and CompactionRL train compression with no criterion at all for what the retained context must contain.

Assimilation as a behavior. In every system above, a return is a mechanism: a summary string arrives and the loop continues. Nothing names, measures, or trains the root’s side of it, reading what the computation produced, at whatever grain the moment needs, and reasoning onward, with everything produced anywhere still reachable. The weaving described above is the surface that makes this possible; the behavior on that surface is the target.

The ladder. Held, handled, latent, lost has no formal occupant, and the latent rung, reachable but never registered, appears nowhere I looked. The closest thing in print is engineering practice: Manus replaces tool outputs with file-system pointers and calls the content externalized rather than lost, which is the held-to-handled move performed by hand. Practitioners are living inside this ladder without a definition of it.

The composite. The authoring line, Voyager through Conductor, and the trajectory-economy line, ABBEL through Context-Folding, are disjoint literatures. No work puts program authorship, delegation, and a sufficiency invariant on the root under one objective. That composite is what this post describes, and it, rather than any single ingredient, is the claim I think survives.

What has to be trained

Placed on the harness untrained, current models delegate but do not meta-reason, and the affinity improves little under prompting, even with detailed, optimized system prompts, reasoning models hold to the habits of the single trajectory. The disposition has to be trained in, and the training is not only subtractive. Taking work off the trajectory is half of it, the other half is new duties, authoring, granting, briefing, weaving, that no model has ever been trained to perform.

The original plan was to train a model that authors policies in a space whose coverage exceeds the decomposition space, and the summer removed the first half of that plan. What remains, and what I think is the more interesting target anyway, is training for the invariant: a model rewarded for keeping sufficiency and minimality together, which is to say rewarded for what it assimilates and for what it declines to carry. How meta-reasoning is enforced, how it is rewarded, how it is discovered at all, are open questions, and we leave them open deliberately. The substrate is more expressive than the one it is compared to, and that is exactly why it must be trained. Developing that training is the program of this work.

Appendix: the experimental program

I am writing this before the program is finished, and the honest state is uneven, so here is what was planned, what has been run, and what has not.

E1, the gradient. Whether policy shape alone, holding the model and the task fixed, moves capability. This part came out clean. On the deduction task the same executor moved from 0.17 to 0.70 across policy designs, a factor of four from authoring alone, the endpoints coming from a six-instance baseline and a ten-instance final. Every number in this post is on the small model I develop against, not yet requalified at the scale I would use for a paper, so I report the gradient as a strong indication rather than a settled measurement. Zhang’s harness results and the Meta-Harness line of work point the same way from a different direction.

E2, the barrier. Whether some task exists where the best policy in the full space beats the best policy under the string contract by a margin that survives a serious attempt at emulation. This part failed, and the verdicts are better named than counted. The duel came in under its own threshold with the gap running the wrong way. The first constructed task had its kill condition fire at two thirds in the wrong direction, then converged at ceiling on the larger model. The second was voided by a floor effect. The third was discarded on audit, a row-level check finding the small model mis-recording between half and two thirds of its own observations, so its four-way tie was noise. A fourth run, a composed policy stacking six mechanisms at once, was discarded before reporting when I found the comparison arm had no parse-retry loop while the constrained arm effectively did, an authoring asymmetry rather than a contract one. And the minimal exhibit for role authorship hit its pre-registered threshold from the wrong side, roles intact at twenty-four of twenty-four against the flattened version’s twenty-two, a difference of 0.083 against a threshold of 0.10, so that axis is behaviorally inert on the shape I tested at the scale I tested it.

I want to be careful about how much all that means. It rules out the gaps I knew how to construct, on the tasks I could afford, at the scale I could afford. It does not rule out the regime I think the theory points at, window-pressured, long-horizon work where the eviction of one’s own past reasoning becomes irreversible, though I am saying that after the null rather than before it, and it is the first thing I would want an unsympathetic reader to press on. I did not get to that regime, it is expensive, and time ran out before the budget did. One axis never got loaded at all, selective granting, and the reason is a design fact rather than a schedule: an agentic policy controls its own globals, so it can quarantine by keeping the sensitive object in a local variable and passing a sanitized string, which closes the naive version of that task before it starts.

E3, authoring. Whether models can author into this space at all, and how that ability varies with what the harness exposes. Not run. This is also the question Alex’s work bears on most directly, since the compositional-generalization result is precisely about training a root to produce the right decompositions, and any serious version of E3 has to be read against it.

A caution about the method, which is the part of this I would defend regardless of the result. Two probes were discarded on audit rather than reported, one because the model was mis-recording most of its own observations and every arm was scoring at chance, and one because I had given the comparison arm a worse deal than the arm I wanted to win. Both would have been publishable-looking results. Neither was real, and the second was mine.

A paper in progress, available here. The experimental program described in the appendix is ongoing, and I will update this post rather than write a second one.
entry.summary: A complementary axis of inference-time scaling that biases the LLM toward abstract computational reasoning. The model authors its computation as policies and keeps its trajectory sufficient and minimal.

entry.title: Forecasting
entry.content:
For the first half of 2026, a good part of our work at Kairosity went into competitive forecasting. It is one of the few tasks where the world itself grades your reasoning, on a schedule, with no partial credit, and frontier models have been closing the gap to human superforecasters fast enough that the competitions got interesting. We entered four. This post is about what we built for each and what the season taught us.

The arenas

The Metaculus AI Benchmark, Spring 2026. A bot-only tournament, a few hundred questions over the season, log-scored against how the world resolves, with the bots benchmarked against the Metaculus community’s own predictions. Alongside it runs MiniBench, back-to-back two-week sprints of about sixty auto-resolving questions, which we used as a fast feedback loop.

ProphetHacks. A 32-hour hackathon out of UChicago in May, run by Sigma Lab, Fleet AI, and Kalshi. You ship an agent that predicts on live Kalshi prediction-market events, and the leaderboard ranks agents by live PnL over a two-week evaluation window. Nothing concentrates the mind like a leaderboard that re-ranks every fifteen seconds.

Prophet Arena. The live benchmark from the LLM-as-a-Prophet group, which continuously evaluates forecasters on real prediction-market events, Brier-scored, across multiple horizons. After the hackathon we kept an agent standing there.

The Upstart Macro Index competition. The quiet one. Monthly forecasts of a macroeconomic index, judged over months rather than minutes.

Metaculus, or the committee that writes code

Our Metaculus bot is a committee of three researchers with one editor, and the rule that defines it is that the researchers are not allowed to hand-wave. Each question first goes through iterative research. A search agent pulls from news and web sources through a single gateway, an analyst critiques what came back, and a supervisor either declares the evidence sufficient or emits targeted sub-queries for another round.

Then three researchers attack the question in parallel, each deliberately running on a different model, so their mistakes decorrelate. Each researcher must anchor on prediction-market and community priors where they exist, and downweight thin ones. Each must state a base rate before updating on news. And each must express its final model as Python. Real scipy distributions, Monte Carlo with at least ten thousand samples, no magic numbers, every constant tagged as researched or assumed. The code actually runs. If predict() fails or returns the wrong outcome keys, the error goes back to the researcher and it tries again.

A consensus agent then reads all three, scores each on analysis quality and model soundness, assigns weights, is allowed to throw a researcher out entirely, fixes unit mistakes (a researcher who says “75” when the question wants 75,000,000 gets corrected, not trusted), and takes the weighted average. Before anything is submitted, there is one last discipline, an overconfidence tax applied exactly once:

\[X = \min(10 - c,\ 0.2\,p)\]

where \(c\) is the researcher’s own certainty out of ten and \(p\) is the leaning-side estimate in percent, and the estimate gets shaved by \(X\) toward the middle. The rule comes with a clause we consider load-bearing: you are not allowed to tune \(c\) to keep the number you already wanted.

The other half of the Metaculus story is operations. The bot runs every twenty minutes, first from CI, then from a server with cron, tmux, and a lockfile so runs never overlap. Every external API sits behind a dispatcher that enforces per-service rate limits with adaptive backoff, because Metaculus wants one request every four seconds and news APIs want less than that. And we have the war story that justifies all of it. One night the dispatcher process died at 03:20 UTC. Cron kept firing every twenty minutes, each run hit connection refused, and by 04:40 the question had closed without our forecast. The forecasting was fine. The plumbing lost the points. In live tournaments, reliability is not an engineering nicety, it is a scoring term.

ProphetHacks, or 32 hours and a bot called GreenieBot

Before writing any code for the hackathon, we studied the field. Metaculus bots post their reasoning publicly, and we had been reading the traces of a strong one called GreenieBot. We pulled its public traces, distilled them into two lists, behaviors to copy and behaviors to avoid, and baked both into our prompts as few-shot examples. Some of those lessons are still in our prompt files verbatim, like the reminder that models systematically underprice questions where a benchmark score is already near the threshold, and the line we quote at each other: overweighting formal caution can be as damaging as overconfidence.

The hackathon agent itself is small and paranoid. One HTTP endpoint. Retrieval is bounded Exa search planned by a cheap model, two rounds, a handful of queries per round, at most ten sources, under a hard 420-second wall clock. Forecasting is two independent forecaster-verifier branches running in parallel, the verifier hunting resolver mistakes, prior misuse, and overconfidence, and a synthesizer that merges the branches without ever smearing to uniform. And if anything anywhere throws, the agent returns a uniform fallback rather than nothing, because completion rate is scored and a missed submission is worse than an honest coin flip. The line from our submission notes: a beautiful forecast that misses the schema is still a failed forecast.

One Kalshi-specific detail cost us real thought. Listed outcomes on a market do not have to sum to one, the resolver semantics are per-label, so the agent preserves calibrated per-label probabilities and refuses to normalize unless the resolver says the outcomes are exhaustive and exclusive. It is exactly the kind of detail that silently costs points if your pipeline helpfully normalizes behind your back.

On the live PnL leaderboard we sat first for a moment. We ended third.

Prophet Arena, or staying live

After the hackathon we took the same core, scrubbed it into a clean deployment, and kept it standing on Prophet Arena, where events keep arriving from real markets and the grading never stops. The engineering brief changes when there is no closing ceremony. Under load testing, three parallel requests complete in about 39 seconds each with both forecast branches running, and the whole pipeline stays comfortably under the ten-minute budget per question. Same philosophy as the hackathon, calibration over confidence, schema over beauty, always answer.

Upstart, or knowing when not to send an agent

The Upstart Macro Index competition asked for monthly index forecasts with uncertainty bands. We tracked the index’s regime, fit AR(1) models on the recent window, and bootstrapped the intervals. The index peaked around 1.67 in late 2023 and read 1.39 in December 2025, with California diverging well below the national line, and our submissions came down to reading monetary policy and sector layoffs correctly, then letting a two-parameter model from a statistics textbook do the arithmetic. Knowing when the right forecaster is not an agent is also a forecasting skill.

What carried over

Across four arenas, the same three lessons kept re-proving themselves.

Reliability is a scoring term. Fallbacks, rate limits, lockfiles, timeouts, completion rate. Nearly every point we lost all season was lost by plumbing, not by reasoning.

Calibration wants machinery, not vibes. The explicit shrink formula, verifiers whose job is to attack overconfidence, market priors as anchors, unit-checking before aggregation. Every one of these exists because we watched a raw model be confidently wrong in a specific, repeatable way.

And the one that became a research question. Ask a strong model the same question in different clothes, a binary here, the same thing as a multiple choice there, and the numbers stop agreeing with each other. Accuracy kept improving all season. Consistency did not. That observation turned into our working paper, Brittle Prophets, where we test whether a causal world model can actually fix this.
entry.summary: The competitions we entered at Kairosity, the agents we built for them, and what live leaderboards taught us about reliability, calibration, and consistency.

entry.title: AFramework
entry.content:
AFramework is an agent framework, that is what the A stands for. I built it at Kairosity, and this is its open-source version. The idea fits in one line: separate the applications that use LLM inference from the inference itself.

Why

Picture one machine’s worth of CPU and RAM, and many applications that all want LLM-driven work done on it. The GPU side of this separation already has its answer: engines like vLLM and SGLang sit between the model and everyone who wants a forward pass, and schedule those passes well. But an agentic workload is not a forward pass. A ReAct-style task is long stretches of I/O, tool calls, API waits, retrieval, braided with bursts of CPU work, and the model call is only one piece of it. For that side of inference there is no shared substrate, so every application builds its own orchestration, its own rate limiting, its own retries, around the same recurring needs.

AFramework is that substrate. An application submits a task over a socket and stops caring. A shared daemon runs it, next to every other application’s tasks, and optimizes the whole load on whatever the box has.

There is also a blunter reason. The popular frameworks in this space break often, LangChain most famously, and the design goal here was the opposite of a framework that does everything: a small daemon with a narrow contract that stays up.

The shape of the system

You do not start AFramework. The first client call that needs it starts the daemon on a Unix socket if one is not already answering, and plugin modules load lazily, only the ones your spec names. For a long-lived deployment you can run the daemon yourself, but nothing requires it.

Work runs in isolated worker processes, real parallelism rather than one event loop pretending. A supervisor health-checks the workers, respawns the dead ones, and drains them on shutdown.

Behavior lives in agent cores. The default core runs a reasoning loop with a model backend and a verifier attached, and custom cores define their own contract with the worker. Everything is specified as plain dicts naming a class, backends are swappable, vLLM, OpenAI, Anthropic, and MCP servers are first class.

The verifier is worth a word, because the name undersells it. Think of it as a monitor that runs over the reasoning each round. It can be an agent in its own right, an LLM that reads the trajectory so far and decides whether the loop should keep going, or it can be a plain condition that fires at a set point: summarize the context once it crosses a token threshold, stop when a criterion is met, structure the final answer before it leaves. It is the hook for watching a reasoning loop while it runs, not only reading what it produced.

Results are durable. A client can submit a task, die, and a different client can later ask for the result and get the same answer, or the same error. Errors are fail-fast and typed: a failing task marks itself failed with a structured error payload, its coroutine dies alone, and the worker keeps serving everything else.

Keeping many apps honest

Sharing a box is a promise applications break on each other, so enforcement is central rather than per-app. Rate limits are Redis-backed token buckets on named resource keys, with circuit breakers over failing resources, and policies declared in one YAML file. Resource keys can be tenant-qualified, acme.openai:gpt-4 style, so “many applications” can also mean “many tenants” without one of them eating the budget of the rest.

The router

Somebody has to decide which worker a task lands on, and round-robin is the answer most systems settle for. AFramework routes by cost. For each candidate worker it estimates the expected latency of this task on that worker, from the worker’s projected CPU and I/O load, with memory pressure and event-loop lag as hard constraints, and a warm-start bonus when a worker has recently run tasks of the same kind. On large fleets it samples a few candidates, power-of-d-choices; on small fleets it simply scans them all.

The part I like most: task costs are not configured anywhere. They are learned online, per task signature, with Bayesian changepoint detection watching for the moment a task’s behavior shifts regime, so the profile follows the workload instead of trusting old evidence. The router deserves a post of its own, so this section is deliberately the short version.

The C++ underneath

The hot path is C++ where it matters, the dispatch queues between router and workers (single-producer, multi-consumer), the scheduler and its worker topology, and the logger’s wire service, each with a Python fallback so the framework still runs unbuilt, just slower. The reasoning is boring and firm: dispatch overhead is paid by every task that moves, so the dispatch path is the one place that must never be the bottleneck.

Using it

import asyncio
from AFramework.agent_core import BaseAgentCoreClient

async def main():
    model_backend = {
        "model_backend_class_name": "VLLMBackend",
        "model": "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507",
    }
    client = BaseAgentCoreClient(agent_id="my_agent")
    client.register_model_backend(**model_backend)
    client.register_verifier(
        verifier_class_name="BaseVerifier",
        model_backend=model_backend,
        max_verification_steps=20,
    )

    session_id = await client.execute_task(
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello world"}],
        stream=True,
    )
    print(f"Task started with Session ID: {session_id}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

That is the whole ceremony. No daemon management, no service files, the framework comes up behind the first call and the task runs in a worker with routing, rate limits, and durability underneath it.

Extending it

The default core is one implementation of a contract, not the only one. Your own agent core is a class behind a decorator:

from AFramework import agent_core, BaseAgentCore

@agent_core
class MyAgentCore(BaseAgentCore):
    # implement register_task / execute_task; define your own loop
    ...

The decorator registers the class by its name, and workers load it lazily when a task asks for it. Tools register the same way, a function behind a hook:

from AFramework import tool_hook

@tool_hook
async def register_my_tools(registry):
    await registry.register_function("my_tool", my_tool_fn, "Description", {})

Model backends and verifiers carry the same @model_backend and @verifier decorators. Everything in the system is a plugin sitting behind a name, which is what lets a task spec be nothing but plain dicts naming the pieces it wants.

A small example

Here is the shape a real app takes: an agent that can factor numbers, because a model is bad at arithmetic and a tool is exact. The tool is an ordinary Python function.

# tools.py
def factorize(n: int) -> list[int]:
    """Return the prime factors of n."""
    factors, d = [], 2
    while d * d <= n:
        while n % d == 0:
            factors.append(d)
            n //= d
        d += 1
    if n > 1:
        factors.append(n)
    return factors

The app wires a backend, a verifier, and that tool onto a client, then asks a question and waits for the answer.

import asyncio
from AFramework.agent_core import BaseAgentCoreClient

model_backend = {
    "model_backend_class_name": "OpenAIBackend",
    "model": "gpt-4o",
}

async def main():
    client = BaseAgentCoreClient(agent_id="factorizer")
    client.register_model_backend(**model_backend)
    client.register_verifier(
        verifier_class_name="BaseVerifier",
        model_backend=model_backend,
        max_verification_steps=10,
    )
    client.register_tool_spec(
        name="factorize",
        import_module="tools",
        attr="factorize",
        description="Return the prime factors of an integer n.",
        parameters={
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"n": {"type": "integer"}},
            "required": ["n"],
        },
    )

    result = await client.execute(
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What are the prime factors of 1001? Use the tool."}],
    )
    print(result["task_result"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

Nothing here starts a server or manages a process. The daemon comes up on the first call, the worker registers the tool from its import path, the agent calls it, the verifier watches the loop, and the answer comes back. The application only ever described what it wanted.

AFramework is open source on GitHub.
entry.summary: Why I built an agent framework that separates applications from LLM inference, and a tour of how it works.

entry.title: PKS: We thought this was hard

link.title: PKS: We thought this was hard

entry.content:
This post is about one section of our paper, Bribery’s Influence on Ranked Aggregation. The paper studies what happens to the Kemeny score under manipulation, bribery, deleting rankings, deleting candidates, and so on. This post is about a problem we were stuck on the longest, a problem called Possible Kemeny Score, which resisted us for a while and then fell to an algorithm so simple we didn’t believe it at first.

Rankings and disagreements

Rank aggregation shows up everywhere. Search engines merge ranked result lists, recommendation systems merge preference orders, panels of judges merge scorecards. The classical way to merge rankings is Kemeny’s rule, from 1959. Given a set of rankings, find the single ranking that disagrees with them the least. It has a nice statistical story too. If voters are noisy observers of one true ranking, the Kemeny ranking is the maximum likelihood estimate of that truth.

“Disagrees the least” is measured by the Kendall tau distance. For two rankings \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\) over the same candidates, it counts the pairs ordered differently:

\[\mathtt{KT}(\pi,\pi') = \big|\{\,\{x,y\} : x \prec_{\pi} y \ \wedge\ y \prec_{\pi'} x \,\}\big|\]

If you draw the two rankings side by side and connect each candidate to itself, the distance is just the number of crossings.

The distance from one ranking \(X\) to a whole set of rankings \(\mathcal{R}\) is the sum, \(\mathtt{KT}(X,\mathcal{R}) = \sum_{R\in\mathcal{R}}\mathtt{KT}(X,R)\).

The problem (intuitively)

Real ballots are incomplete. A reviewer ranks the five papers they actually read. A user ranks the movies they have seen. So suppose the rankings you are given are partial, and suppose someone hands you a target ranking \(X\) over all the candidates and a number \(k\), and asks:

Possible Kemeny Score. Given a candidate set \(\mathcal{C}\), a set of partial rankings \(\mathcal{R}\), a full ranking \(X\), and an integer \(k\), can the partial rankings be completed so that the total Kendall tau distance of \(X\) from the completed rankings is at most \(k\)?

Completing a ranking means inserting the missing candidates anywhere you like, without touching the relative order of the candidates already ranked.

In other words, is there a completion of the evidence under which \(X\) scores at most \(k\)? It is the optimist’s question, and it is also the auditor’s question. Given incomplete preference data, what is the best score this target could possibly have?

Why we thought it was hard

Everything in this problem’s neighborhood is hard. Computing the Kemeny score is NP-complete (Bartholdi, Tovey & Trick, 1989). It is NP-hard already for four rankings, and the case of three rankings has been open for years (Dwork, Kumar, Naor & Sivakumar, 2001; Biedl, Brandenburg & Deng, 2009). The corresponding manipulation questions for Kemeny Consensus are coNP-complete and \(\Sigma_2^p\)-complete (Fitzsimmons & Hemaspaandra, 2021). And the most widely studied problem of this shape, the Possible Winner problem, where partial votes are completed to make a favorite candidate win, is NP-hard for most common voting rules (Xia & Conitzer, 2011). All of this pointed at the same thing: the problem is hard. Or so we thought.

But our stuckness was more concrete than that. Try to solve it. You have to insert the missing candidates into a ballot, and there are two levels of freedom, and both looked unmanageable.

First level. In what relative order do the missing candidates go in? You might guess “in the order \(X\) ranks them,” but we had no reason to believe that. The candidates already sitting in the ballot do not agree with \(X\), they are in whatever order the voter put them. So maybe following \(X\)’s order among the new candidates generates extra disagreements against those already-placed candidates, and some other order does better. We could not rule that out, and without it we had nothing to hold on to.

Second level. Even if you somehow knew the right relative order, where do the candidates actually go? Place the first one at some position. Nothing guarantees that position is consistent with any optimal completion. It felt like every placement decision could poison the ones after it, which is exactly the situation where you expect to need search, and search over interleavings is exponential.

We could not find an approach.

The first insight

The first insight was that the natural guess turns out to be right. In any optimal completion, the inserted candidates appear in \(X\)’s order relative to each other.

Lemma 1. Let \(\hat{R}\) be an optimal extension of \(R\). Then \(\hat{R}\) and \(X\) agree over the inserted candidates.

The proof is an exchange argument. Suppose two inserted candidates \(c, c'\) sit in the wrong order, \(c \prec_X c'\) but \(c' \prec_{\hat{R}} c\). Swap them. The pair \(\{c,c'\}\) itself now agrees with \(X\), so that is one disagreement gone. For any candidate \(w\) caught between them, check the three places \(w\) can sit in \(X\): before both, between them, after both. Walking the cases, every disagreement the swap creates is matched by one it removes, and the between case removes two. The distance never goes up, and the pair itself strictly improves. So an out-of-order pair can never be in an optimal completion.

This kills the first level of freedom completely. The internal order of the insertions is not a choice, it is \(X\)’s order. What remains is only the question of positions.

The second insight, and the algorithm

The position problem was still standing. Insert the candidates in \(X\)’s order, fine, but put the first one somewhere and you still have no guarantee that any optimal completion has it there.

The algorithm that resolves it looks like this.

Take the missing candidates in \(X\)’s order. Insert each one at the leftmost position that minimizes its disagreements with the already-ranked candidates. And after you place a candidate, never look to the left of it again, the pointer \(l\) only moves right.

A small example. Let \(X = a \prec b \prec c \prec d \prec e\) and let the ballot be \(R = c \prec a \prec e\), so \(b\) and \(d\) are missing and get inserted in that order.

For \(b\), the four available slots cost \(1, 2, 1, 2\) disagreements against the fixed candidates. Positions \(0\) and \(2\) tie, so the leftmost wins and \(b\) goes first: \(b \prec c \prec a \prec e\). For \(d\), the slots from the pointer onward cost \(2, 1, 0, 1\), so \(d\) goes after \(a\): \(b \prec c \prec a \prec d \prec e\). Total distance to \(X\): the ballot’s own inversion \((c,a)\), plus \(1\) for \(b\), plus \(0\) for \(d\). You can check by brute force that no completion of \(R\) does better.

Why it works

Two facts carry the proof.

The first is a monotonicity that we did not expect. Suppose a placed candidate \(\Pi(i)\) does at least as well further right, at some position \(t_f\) that minimizes its disagreements among the positions after it. Then you can push it there, dragging along every later insertion sitting in between, and never pay for it. The engine is a pointwise inequality. When \(\Pi(i)\) moves one step right past a fixed candidate, the change in its disagreements with the fixed candidates is \(+1\) or \(-1\). And for every later insertion \(\Pi(\ell)\), with \(\ell > i\),

\[\Delta\,\Pi(\ell) \;\leq\; \Delta\,\Pi(i).\]

The reason is the agreement from Lemma 1. If the step saves a disagreement for \(\Pi(i)\), the fixed candidate it passes comes before \(\Pi(i)\) in \(X\), and since \(\Pi(i) \prec_X \Pi(\ell)\), it also comes before \(\Pi(\ell)\), so the same step saves one for \(\Pi(\ell)\) too. The later candidates ride along for free. Summed over the whole journey to \(t_f\), nobody’s total goes up.

The second fact is the induction that turns this into optimality. At every step of the algorithm there exists an optimal completion that agrees with everything placed so far. If the optimal completion has the current candidate further left than the algorithm put it, move it right using the free-ride lemma. If it has it further right, moving it left to the algorithm’s position costs nothing, because the algorithm’s position was a minimizer. Either way there is an optimal completion matching the algorithm’s prefix, and at the end, matching its entire output.

Ballots do not interact, the total distance is a sum, so running the procedure on each ballot independently is optimal overall. The whole thing runs in \(\mathcal{O}(n \cdot m^3)\), for \(n\) ballots over \(m\) candidates.

In hindsight

For a long time we were convinced this problem was hard, and the honest reason is that we had not found the two lemmas. Without the agreement lemma there is no order to insert in, and without the free-ride inequality no placement is safe to commit to. Both freedoms looked like they demanded search. The two symmetries we discovered are what make a greedy algorithm the solution.

It is a strange table our paper ends up with. For Kemeny Consensus, these manipulation questions sit at coNP-complete and \(\Sigma_2^p\)-complete where their status is known at all. For Kemeny Score, the decision version, all of these turn out polynomial, bribery via a reduction to Knapsack, ranking deletion, swap bribery, and the problem in this post. Same rule, same manipulative actions, a complexity gulf between the optimisation and decision questions.

The three-voter Kemeny score, whether it is polynomial or NP-hard, is still open, and so is every Kemeny Winner column of our table.

Read the full paper on arXiv.
entry.summary: How a problem we couldn't crack for weeks fell to a greedy algorithm, from our paper on manipulating the Kemeny score.

entry.title: Fixing Table Bounding Boxes with RL

link.title: Fixing Table Bounding Boxes with RL

entry.content:
At Decimal Point Analytics I work with financial documents, and financial documents contain a lot of tables. This problem was plaguing us: our docket pipeline at the time genuinely struggled with tables. Detection comes first, a model draws bounding boxes around rows and cells, and everything downstream trusts those boxes. The boxes drift, rows merge, phantom rows appear, and long tables make it worse, by the bottom of one it gets hard to make sense of anything. Every bad box becomes a corrupted record two stages later.

The usual fix is to fine-tune the detector with more labeled pages, and labeling table geometry is miserable work. So we tried a different route: keep the detector, and train a second model to repair its output. It did not start from scratch. The starting point was the prediction from Surya OCR, a very powerful OCR at the time, and the neural network learned to correct the mistakes in those bounding boxes.

The idea

The environment is a page. The state is the detector’s boxes laid over the words it found. The network’s actions are small edits, nudge a box edge, delete a row box, halt when done. An episode starts from what Surya produced and ends with what the network left behind, and the reward measures whether the boxes ended up agreeing with the words on the page.

That reward came in two designs. The first is geometric, computed from the page itself: how cleanly the row boxes cut between word clusters, how many words end up owned by exactly one row, whether a deleted row was one the words never needed. That version is implemented in the open code. The second design replaces geometry with judgment, an OpenAI vision model looks at the boxed page and scores it. The applied version went that way, and the honest note from the code’s own header is that it works even when the judge is somewhat jank.

It worked a lot better than we expected, the repaired boxes showed real gains over the detector’s own, and a version of this went into use internally at DPA. The environments are C, built as PufferLib Ocean environments and trained with PufferLib’s PPO, which is what made iterating on a page-sized state cheap enough to try ideas like this at all.
entry.summary: Teaching a neural network to repair a table detector's bounding boxes, with geometric rewards in the open version and a vision model as the judge in the applied one.

entry.title: PolyTM: learning polynomial-time oracles
entry.content:
PolyTM is a reinforcement learning environment I built inside PufferLib, around one question: can a neural network learn to discover algorithms? Not to answer a problem instance, but to produce the procedure that answers every instance, and to do it in polynomial time.

The idea

The environment is a machine. There is a tape of integers holding the problem, and the agent does not output answers, it outputs instructions: pick two cells, pick an operation, add or multiply, pick a cell to write the result into. Step by step it edits the tape, and when it halts, the reward depends on whether the designated result cells hold the right values. The network is not being trained to know the answer. It is being trained to build the computation that produces the answer.

The environment also keeps the two honest ledgers of computation: how many steps an episode took and how many cells it wrote. Running time and space, logged for every episode, because an algorithm that exists but wastes the tape is not the algorithm we are looking for.

The committed version is this register machine. The version it was growing into is a proper multi-tape Turing machine, separate work, state, and result tapes, read heads with observation windows, an alphabet, penalties for refusing to halt. Same idea, stricter machine. The heads and their windows exist for a blunt reason, the observation vector cannot be the whole tape once the tape grows, so the agent reads through small windows around its heads and has to learn to move them, which is, of course, exactly what a Turing machine does. We experimented along that axis, more heads with narrow views against fewer heads with wider ones, because visibility was the budget everything else had to fit inside.

The tasks across versions ran from summing and binary addition to sorting, each instance random every episode. A Sudoku solver was planned as the showpiece and never came through.

The policy that drives it is a transformer over the tape. Each integer cell is read as its bytes, its sign, and a hashed identity, embedded and attended over, with an LSTM carrying memory across steps, trained with PufferLib 3.0’s PPO. The one thing this setup refuses to do is memorize instances: the problems are random every episode, so the only thing worth learning is the procedure.

Where it came from

The question came out of algorithms, not machine learning. Working with Dr. Pallavi Jain on ranked aggregation, the open problem in the air was EFX, whether an envy-free-up-to-any-good allocation always exists, known for three agents and open from four onward, and she encouraged me to hunt for a counterexample. Hunting for counterexamples and hunting for algorithms are the same kind of search, discrete, enormous, and allergic to gradients, and I wanted to know whether a learned searcher could walk spaces like that. The first version of the environment says so outright. Before the general tape machine there was poly_time, and its problem was literally a fair-division instance, four agents, a random utility matrix over the items, and the machine’s output was an allocation with a halt flag. PolyTM was what it generalized into, the small, controlled version of the question.

It did work, for some of it. The network learned to compose correct computations for the arithmetic tasks, and the work pushed further from there. What it did not give me is the thing I wanted next: you can watch the tape and see that it computes, but not read back what algorithm it found. Explainability was the planned second half, extracting the discovered procedure from the trained policy, and it stayed planned.

Edit: I did not see it at the time, but this was an early run at the idea I now work on. A model that, given a task, produces the computation that solves it rather than grinding out the answer itself, that is the whole shape of my current work on meta-reasoning in language models. PolyTM was the same bet, placed on a tape instead of a trajectory.
entry.summary: An RL environment where a neural network learns to write the computation that solves a problem, instead of guessing the answer.
